title: How to Plan an Okavango Field Course for University Conservation Students
meta_title: Okavango Field Course Planning for University Groups
meta_description: Plan an Okavango field course: Maun base, research permits, Moremi fees, group logistics, a 12-day route and per-student costs for university groups.
excerpt: An Okavango field course gives university students wetland ecology, wildlife and conservation fieldwork in Botswana. Here is how to plan the base, permits, route and budget.
content:
An okavango field course takes university students out of the lecture hall and into one of Africa's largest inland deltas, usually for 10 to 14 days based in Maun, Botswana. Students study flood-pulse ecology, wetland birds, large herbivores and community conservation by mokoro, on foot and from open vehicles in Moremi and Khwai.

Lecturers who want to run one face a short list of hard questions: where to base the group, whether students need a research permit, how to move 15 or 20 people through roadless swamp, and what it will cost per head. This guide answers each of them, and our student and university study tour safaris page explains how we build trips like this for faculty and study-abroad offices.

Quick Facts

  • Gateway town: Maun, about 2 hours 10 minutes by air from Johannesburg, with daily scheduled flights
  • Ideal length: 10 to 14 days on the ground, so an Okavango field course has time for data collection and analysis
  • Core sites: Maun and the Okavango Research Institute, the mokoro channels, Moremi Game Reserve and the Khwai area
  • Moremi entry: DWNP park fee plus a pre-booked campsite; a proposed non-resident rise from P380 to P500 is on hold (checked November 2026)
  • Research permit: Free, about ten working days, apply at least one month before travel if students collect data
  • Best months: June to September, when the flood is high and the weather is dry and cool
  • Group size that works: 12 to 20 students plus two or three staff

What Can Students Study on an Okavango Field Course?

The Okavango Delta suits wetland ecology, hydrology, large-mammal behaviour, ornithology and community-based conservation better than almost anywhere in southern Africa. Water from the Angolan highlands floods a desert basin each year, so students watch an ecosystem expand and contract within a single season.

That annual flood pulse is the teaching hook of any Okavango field course: the delta is at its wettest in the dry winter, months after the local rains, so students can track water, plants and animals along one transect as the flood moves. Our Okavango Delta safari planner explains the flood calendar in more detail for pre-departure reading.

Which modules suit an okavango field course?

Conservation biology, freshwater ecology, environmental science, geography and wildlife management are the natural fit for an okavango field course. Tourism management and development studies work well too, especially if you add a village visit and a session with a camp manager on how concession fees reach local trusts.

Keep the projects on an Okavango field course small and repeatable. Bird point counts from a mokoro, dung counts along a fixed walking route, waterhole watches from a vehicle and simple water-quality readings all produce usable data in a few days without specialist kit.

Maun and the Okavango Research Institute as a Base

Maun is the right base because it has the airport, supermarkets, fuel, a hospital and the University of Botswana's Okavango Research Institute (ORI). Groups usually spend their first two nights and last night here for briefings, lectures and kit checks.

ORI shows what kind of academic support exists locally. Its own Introduction to Wetland Research course ran for about seven weeks in Maun in June and July 2026 for University of Botswana students, combining classroom work, field and lab projects, data analysis and presentations to institute staff, with a self-catering tented camp for participants (checked November 2026). Visiting universities wanting guest lectures or lab time should approach the institute directly, well ahead of travel.

Where Should the Group Go Inside the Delta?

Most university groups split their time between three zones: the mokoro channels reached from Maun, Moremi Game Reserve on the eastern side of the delta, and the Khwai area just outside Moremi's North Gate. Together they cover permanent water, seasonal floodplain and dry woodland within a few hours' drive.

The mokoro block is where an Okavango field course meets the delta at water level: polers push canoes through reed channels to island camps, at a pace that suits bird counts and aquatic plant work. Our 3-day Okavango Delta mokoro tour follows this pattern, with two nights on a remote island and guided walks each day.

Moremi and Khwai provide the large-mammal side of the course, with campsites at South Gate, Xakanaxa, Third Bridge and North Gate. Khwai, outside the reserve, allows night drives and walking that are restricted inside Moremi.

Plan around flood damage

Floods shape access too: when Moremi reopened in April 2026 after weather-related closures, Third Bridge stayed closed and the Khwai to Xakanaxa track was impassable for a time. Build a backup site into every Okavango field course plan and confirm route status a few weeks before arrival.

Permits, Health and Paperwork

The main paperwork for a university group is a research permit if students collect data, valid passports, any visas their nationalities need and health preparation for a malaria area. Start this three to four months before departure, alongside your university's own risk assessment.

Does an Okavango field course need a research permit?

An Okavango field course that gathers research data needs a Botswana research permit. The Government of Botswana research permit page says individuals conducting research must apply to the ministry or department their work relates to, with an endorsement letter from the sponsoring institution, CVs with passport details for every researcher and a research proposal. The permit is free, processing takes about ten working days, and non-residents should apply at least a month before travel (checked November 2026).

A purely observational teaching trip sits in a grey area, so send your course outline to the relevant department and ask in writing. If students will publish or submit their results for credit, treat it as research and apply.

Malaria and entry rules

Northern Botswana carries the country's highest malaria risk. NHS Fit for Travel guidance on Botswana names Ngamiland and Chobe as the high-risk districts, with transmission year-round but highest from November to June, and advises antimalarial tablets plus bite avoidance there (checked November 2026). Each student should see a travel clinic six to eight weeks before departure.

Visa rules depend on nationality, so collect every passport early and check each against Botswana's official immigration guidance before booking flights.

Group Size, Vehicles, Rooming and Safety

A group of 12 to 20 students with two or three staff is the sweet spot for an Okavango field course. It fills three open safari vehicles, keeps mokoro fleets manageable and gives every vehicle a staff member for supervision and data checks.

Each mokoro carries two passengers plus a poler, so 18 students need nine canoes, which need booking well ahead. Open 4x4 safari vehicles typically seat six to nine, and we keep one seat free for kit. Our guide to organising a group safari covers how we size vehicles and staff for groups.

Rooming on a camping-based Okavango field course is simple: two students per dome tent, staff tents at each end of camp, gender-separated tent lines and a clear rule about leaving tents at night. In Maun, a guesthouse with twin rooms keeps the group together.

Why a private group trip beats joining strangers

A private Okavango field course runs on your fieldwork schedule, not a fixed game-drive timetable. You can sit for an hour at one waterhole, repeat the same transect each morning and hold seminars in camp, none of which works on a shared tour with guests who want lions.

It is also easier to supervise: your staff, our guide and the camp crew are the only adults with the group, and the emergency plan covers your students alone. Our group safaris are built on this private model.

A Sample 12-Day Okavango Field Course Route

A 12-day Okavango field course can move from orientation in Maun to the mokoro channels, then into Moremi and Khwai for the main data block, finishing back in Maun to analyse results. The table below is a starting framework that faculty can adjust to their modules.

DaysLocationTeaching focus
1-2MaunArrival, safety briefing, Okavango ecology lectures, kit checks
3-5Mokoro channels and island campBird point counts, aquatic plants, guided walks, poler-led natural history
6-8Moremi Game Reserve (South Gate or Xakanaxa)Herbivore counts, waterhole watches, floodplain vegetation transects
9-10Khwai community areaNight drive, walking, community conservation and concession revenue
11MaunData entry, analysis, group presentations
12MaunDeparture

Groups with four extra days can continue through Savuti to Chobe National Park and Kasane for elephant ecology and a river system. Our 7-day Moremi, Khwai and Savuti safari shows the overland route, and our Okavango Delta vs Chobe comparison helps faculty decide whether the extension earns its days.

When to run it

June to September is the best window for an Okavango field course. The flood is high, days are dry and cool, nights can drop close to freezing, and malaria risk is lower than in the rains. Our guide to the best time to visit Botswana covers each month, including the hot build-up of October and the green season from December.

How Much Does an Okavango Field Course Cost per Student?

An Okavango field course usually costs between about US$250 and US$450 per student per day on a mobile camping model, before international flights, and far more if the group stays in permanent safari camps. These are estimates per person: the final figure depends on group size, season and how many nights are spent inside Moremi.

Park fees are a modest part of the total but are in flux. The Botswana Daily News reported in February 2026 a proposed rise in the non-resident park fee from P380 to P500, and the increase was later put on hold (checked November 2026). Campsite operators inside Moremi charge their own fees on top, so confirm the DWNP tariff before you set a student price.

Cost itemEstimate per studentNotes
Moremi park and campsite feesConfirm when bookingDWNP fee under review: proposed non-resident rise from P380 to P500 on hold (checked November 2026)
Mobile camping in Moremi and KhwaiAbout US$200 to US$350 a dayEstimate: guide, vehicle, crew, tents, meals, campsite fees
Mokoro and island camp (3 days)From US$715 for 3 daysOur 3-day mokoro tour price per adult, from Maun
Maun accommodationAbout US$60 to US$150 a nightEstimate: guesthouse twin room, depends on season
Permanent tented campsAbout US$600 a night and upEstimate: suits staff-led alumni trips more than student budgets

Per-student costs on an Okavango field course fall as the group grows, because the guide, vehicles and crew are shared, so recruit to vehicle capacity. Staff places are usually priced into the student fee.

Insider Tips

  • Book campsites first: Moremi entry needs a confirmed campsite booking, and popular sites fill for July and August a year ahead
  • Pack for cold mornings: June and July nights in the delta can drop close to freezing, so students need fleeces and warm sleeping bags
  • Brief the polers: Explain the sampling plan to the polers and guides on day one, as they know where the birds and animals will be
  • Plan a buffer day: Floods and sand tracks slow transfers, so leave one flexible day before the final presentations

Frequently Asked Questions

How long should an Okavango field course be?

An Okavango field course works best at 10 to 14 days on the ground. That gives two or three days in Maun for briefings and lectures, a mokoro block in the delta, four or five nights of camping in Moremi or Khwai for data collection, and a final day for analysis and presentations before students fly home.

Do students need a research permit for an Okavango field course?

Students need a Botswana research permit if the Okavango field course collects data for research. The government says individuals conducting research must apply to the ministry or department their work relates to, with an endorsement letter, CVs and a proposal. It is free and takes about ten working days (checked November 2026). Confirm whether a teaching-only course needs one.

What does it cost to enter Moremi Game Reserve?

Moremi Game Reserve fees are set by Botswana's Department of Wildlife and National Parks and are under review. Government news reported in February 2026 a proposed rise in the non-resident fee from P380 to P500, which was later put on hold (checked November 2026). Campsite operators charge separately, so confirm the current tariff before you set a student price.

When is the best time for an Okavango field course?

The best time for an Okavango field course is June to September, when the flood is high, the weather is dry and cool, and malaria risk is lower than in the wet season. That window also suits northern-hemisphere summer terms. November to March brings rain, heat and the highest malaria risk in Ngamiland.

How many students can join one Okavango field course?

Most groups run best with 12 to 20 students and two or three staff. Each mokoro carries two passengers and a poler, and open safari vehicles seat six to nine, so a group of that size fits three vehicles and a small mokoro fleet. Larger cohorts can split into two groups running a day apart.

Final Thoughts

A strong Okavango field course starts in Maun, spends a few quiet days on the water and puts most of its time into Moremi and Khwai, with permits, campsites and malaria advice sorted months ahead. Run it in the June to September flood and keep the projects simple enough to finish in camp.
